---
title: "05 · Case Study: Can a NIRS Scanner Replace the Oven to Measure Cassava Dry Matter?"
author: "Maria Jose Ospina"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, fig.path = "figures/"
)
```

## The question

**Dry matter content** is one of the most important traits in cassava breeding: roots with more dry matter give more starch and are worth more to farmers and processors. Breeding programs measure it on thousands of plots every season, so the method matters.

| Method | Variable | How it works | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oven drying** | `DM_raw` | Weigh a root sample, dry it in an oven and weigh it again | Reference method, but slow |
| **Specific gravity** | `DM_gravity` | Weigh the roots in air and in water | Fast and cheap, but indirect |
| **NIRS** | `DM_nirs` | Scan the sample with near-infrared spectroscopy | Very fast, but needs calibration |

**Can the faster methods replace the oven?** This report compares them with correlation, regression and agreement analysis, and checks whether they would lead a breeder to select the same varieties.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

method_colors <- c("Oven" = "#555555", "NIRS" = "#0072B2", "Specific gravity" = "#D55E00")
```

## 1. Data

```{r load}
cassava <- read_csv("data/cassava_dry_matter.csv") |>
  mutate(
    trial     = str_extract(plot_name, "^[^_]+_[^_]+"),
    location  = str_split_i(plot_name, "_", 2),
    replicate = str_extract(plot_name, "rep\\d")
  )

glimpse(cassava)
```

The dataset has **`r nrow(cassava)` field plots** of **`r n_distinct(cassava$accession_name)` cassava accessions**, grown in **`r n_distinct(cassava$trial)` trials** at two locations, with two replicates each.

```{r coverage}
cassava |>
  group_by(trial) |>
  summarise(
    plots      = n(),
    oven       = sum(!is.na(DM_raw)),
    nirs       = sum(!is.na(DM_nirs)),
    gravity    = sum(!is.na(DM_gravity))
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Trial", "Plots", "Oven", "NIRS", "Specific gravity"))
```

One trial was measured **only with specific gravity**, so every comparison against the oven uses the plots where both methods are available.

```{r paired}
nirs_pairs    <- cassava |> drop_na(DM_raw, DM_nirs)
gravity_pairs <- cassava |> drop_na(DM_raw, DM_gravity)
```

- Oven vs. NIRS: **`r nrow(nirs_pairs)` plots**
- Oven vs. specific gravity: **`r nrow(gravity_pairs)` plots**

### Distribution of each method

```{r distributions}
cassava |>
  pivot_longer(c(DM_raw, DM_nirs, DM_gravity), names_to = "method", values_to = "dm") |>
  filter(!is.na(dm)) |>
  mutate(method = recode(method, DM_raw = "Oven", DM_nirs = "NIRS", DM_gravity = "Specific gravity"),
         method = factor(method, levels = names(method_colors))) |>
  ggplot(aes(dm, color = method, fill = method)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.15, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = method_colors) +
  labs(title = "Dry matter measured by each method",
       x = "Dry matter (%)", y = "Density", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

The oven and NIRS curves almost overlap, while specific gravity is shifted to lower values.

## 2. Correlation

```{r correlation}
cor_matrix <- cassava |>
  select(Oven = DM_raw, NIRS = DM_nirs, `Specific gravity` = DM_gravity) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

round(cor_matrix, 3)
```

```{r scatter, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
bind_rows(
  nirs_pairs    |> transmute(oven = DM_raw, value = DM_nirs,    method = "NIRS"),
  gravity_pairs |> transmute(oven = DM_raw, value = DM_gravity, method = "Specific gravity")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(oven, value, color = method)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(15, 55), ylim = c(15, 55)) +
  labs(title = "Each method against the oven (reference)",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: perfect agreement · Black line: fitted regression",
       x = "Oven dry matter (%)", y = "Method dry matter (%)")
```

NIRS points follow the line of perfect agreement closely; specific gravity points are much more scattered.

## 3. Regression models

```{r models}
model_nirs    <- lm(DM_nirs ~ DM_raw, data = nirs_pairs)
model_gravity <- lm(DM_gravity ~ DM_raw, data = gravity_pairs)

summary(model_nirs)
summary(model_gravity)
```

```{r model-table}
model_summary <- function(model, name) {
  s <- summary(model)
  tibble(
    method    = name,
    intercept = coef(model)[1],
    slope     = coef(model)[2],
    r_squared = s$r.squared,
    rmse      = sqrt(mean(residuals(model)^2))
  )
}

models <- bind_rows(
  model_summary(model_nirs, "NIRS"),
  model_summary(model_gravity, "Specific gravity")
)

kable(models, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Method", "Intercept (β₀)", "Slope (β₁)", "R²", "RMSE (points)"))
```

```{r r2}
r2_nirs    <- models$r_squared[models$method == "NIRS"]
r2_gravity <- models$r_squared[models$method == "Specific gravity"]
```

- **NIRS** explains **`r round(r2_nirs * 100)`%** of the variation in oven dry matter, with a slope close to 1.
- **Specific gravity** explains only **`r round(r2_gravity * 100)`%**.

### Prediction: oven dry matter of 30%

The class assignment asked what NIRS value corresponds to a sample with **30% dry matter in the oven**.

```{r predict-30}
pred_30 <- predict(model_nirs, tibble(DM_raw = 30), interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
pred_30
```

A sample with 30% dry matter in the oven is expected to read about **`r round(pred_30[, "fit"], 1)`%** on the NIRS, and a single sample would usually fall between `r round(pred_30[, "lwr"], 1)`% and `r round(pred_30[, "upr"], 1)`%.

In practice the question is usually the reverse: the NIRS gives a reading and the breeder wants the oven-equivalent value. That calibration model is fitted the other way around:

```{r calibration}
calibration <- lm(DM_raw ~ DM_nirs, data = nirs_pairs)
oven_from_30 <- predict(calibration, tibble(DM_nirs = 30), interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
oven_from_30
```

A NIRS reading of 30% corresponds to an oven value of about **`r round(oven_from_30[, "fit"], 1)`%** (95% prediction interval: `r round(oven_from_30[, "lwr"], 1)`–`r round(oven_from_30[, "upr"], 1)`%).

## 4. Agreement: Bland-Altman analysis

A high correlation does not mean two methods give the **same values**: one could be consistently higher. The Bland-Altman plot shows the **difference** between each method and the oven against their **average**.

- **Bias:** the mean difference (does the method over- or underestimate?).
- **Limits of agreement:** bias ± 1.96 × SD of the differences, the range where 95% of differences fall.

```{r bland-altman-stats}
agreement <- bind_rows(
  nirs_pairs    |> transmute(method = "NIRS", mean = (DM_raw + DM_nirs) / 2, diff = DM_nirs - DM_raw),
  gravity_pairs |> transmute(method = "Specific gravity", mean = (DM_raw + DM_gravity) / 2, diff = DM_gravity - DM_raw)
)

limits <- agreement |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    bias  = mean(diff),
    lower = bias - 1.96 * sd(diff),
    upper = bias + 1.96 * sd(diff),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(limits, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Method", "Bias (points)", "Lower limit", "Upper limit"))
```

```{r bland-altman, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(agreement, aes(mean, diff, color = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(data = limits, aes(yintercept = bias), linewidth = 0.9, color = "black") +
  geom_hline(data = limits, aes(yintercept = lower), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_hline(data = limits, aes(yintercept = upper), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_color_manual(values = method_colors) +
  labs(title = "Bland-Altman: difference from the oven",
       subtitle = "Solid line: bias · Dashed lines: 95% limits of agreement",
       x = "Average of method and oven (%)", y = "Method − oven (points)")
```

```{r limits-values}
lim_n <- limits |> filter(method == "NIRS")
lim_g <- limits |> filter(method == "Specific gravity")
```

- **NIRS** has almost no bias (`r sprintf("%+.2f", lim_n$bias)` points), and 95% of its readings fall within `r round(lim_n$lower, 1)` to `r sprintf("%+.1f", lim_n$upper)` points of the oven.
- **Specific gravity** underestimates by **`r round(abs(lim_g$bias), 1)` points** on average, and its limits are much wider (`r round(lim_g$lower, 1)` to `r sprintf("%+.1f", lim_g$upper)` points).

### Is the result consistent across trials?

```{r by-trial}
cassava |>
  drop_na(DM_raw) |>
  group_by(trial) |>
  summarise(
    plots           = n(),
    r_nirs          = cor(DM_raw, DM_nirs, use = "complete.obs"),
    r_gravity       = cor(DM_raw, DM_gravity, use = "complete.obs"),
    bias_nirs       = mean(DM_nirs - DM_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    bias_gravity    = mean(DM_gravity - DM_raw, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2,
        col.names = c("Trial", "Plots", "r NIRS", "r gravity", "Bias NIRS", "Bias gravity"))
```

NIRS behaves the same way in every trial, while the performance of specific gravity changes from one trial to another.

## 5. Would the breeder select the same varieties?

In breeding, what matters is often the **ranking**: which accessions have the highest dry matter and move on to the next stage. Here the accessions are averaged across plots and the **top 10%** chosen by each method is compared with the top 10% chosen by the oven.

```{r selection}
accessions <- cassava |>
  drop_na(DM_raw) |>
  group_by(accession_name) |>
  summarise(across(c(DM_raw, DM_nirs, DM_gravity), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
  drop_na()

k <- round(nrow(accessions) * 0.10)

top_oven    <- accessions |> slice_max(DM_raw, n = k, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(accession_name)
top_nirs    <- accessions |> slice_max(DM_nirs, n = k, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(accession_name)
top_gravity <- accessions |> slice_max(DM_gravity, n = k, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(accession_name)

selection <- tibble(
  method        = c("NIRS", "Specific gravity"),
  selected      = k,
  same_as_oven  = c(length(intersect(top_nirs, top_oven)), length(intersect(top_gravity, top_oven))),
  spearman_rank = c(cor(accessions$DM_raw, accessions$DM_nirs, method = "spearman"),
                    cor(accessions$DM_raw, accessions$DM_gravity, method = "spearman"))
) |>
  mutate(agreement = same_as_oven / selected)

kable(selection, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Method", "Accessions selected", "Same as oven", "Rank correlation (Spearman)", "Agreement"))
```

```{r selection-plot}
selection |>
  ggplot(aes(method, agreement, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(same_as_oven, " of ", selected)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = method_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Top 10% accessions that match the oven's selection",
       x = NULL, y = "Agreement with oven")
```

Choosing the best `r k` of `r nrow(accessions)` accessions with **NIRS** would keep **`r selection$same_as_oven[1]`** of the oven's picks; with **specific gravity**, only **`r selection$same_as_oven[2]`**.

## Conclusions

- **NIRS can replace the oven for routine screening.** It explains `r round(r2_nirs * 100)`% of the oven's variation, has practically no bias, and would select most of the same top accessions.
- **Specific gravity is not a good substitute** for precise measurements: it underestimates dry matter by about `r round(abs(lim_g$bias), 1)` points and disagrees much more, although it can still help to discard clearly poor roots quickly.
- **Recommended practice:** use NIRS for large numbers of plots and keep oven drying on a subset of samples each season to check and recalibrate the NIRS.

### Limitations

- The comparison only uses plots where both methods were measured; one trial had no oven or NIRS data.
- The NIRS calibration is specific to these trials; a new environment or new germplasm could need recalibration.
